chrome.title: Mercury on the Home Screen: Building the Liquid Metal Y2K Icon Pack
chrome.subtitle: Around the year 2000 every gadget wanted to look like a puddle of chrome. We brought that gleam to Android.
chrome.description: How we made Liquid Metal, a Y2K Android icon pack of inflated mirror metal icons with a sharp horizon, ten tile colours and 2,900+ icons.
chrome.intro: Think of a 2000s MP3 player, a translucent phone or a glossy website button, and you probably see chrome. Liquid Metal is our love letter to that look: an Android icon pack where every symbol is a swollen blob of mirror metal.
chrome.style_h: Poured metal with a razor horizon
chrome.style_p: Each symbol is one smooth, inflated shape with a dark ink edge, so it stays clear against the glow behind it. Blue sky reflects in the upper half, warm ground in the lower half, and a few hot white highlights mark where the light hits hardest. Separate parts of a symbol get their own tint and a thin dark seam, which keeps a phone, a camera or a calculator readable at launcher size.
chrome.make_p: Real chrome reflects its surroundings, and a flat icon has no surroundings. So the renderer invents a tiny world around every shape: a sky, a sharp horizon line and a warm floor, then bends it over the inflated surface. The horizon was the hard part. Too soft and the metal looks like plastic, too hard and it turns into a stripe. Behind the metal sits a deep glowing tile, smooth, with sunburst rays or with a faint perspective grid, and small sparkles drift in the corners.
chrome.colours: ten tile colours: cobalt, bubblegum, gold, lime, ruby, violet, ocean, slate, amber and mint, plus a near-black onyx for the darkest apps

circuit.title: A Green City of Copper: Making the Circuit Board Icon Pack
circuit.subtitle: Open the back of any gadget and you find a tiny city. We put that view on your home screen.
circuit.description: The story of Circuit Board, an Android icon pack with gold-plated copper symbols, vias and silkscreen on ten board colours, with 2,900+ icons.
circuit.intro: Every phone is full of circuit boards and almost nobody ever sees one. Circuit Board turns the view inside a gadget into an Android icon pack: shiny gold symbols laid out like a printed circuit, on a coloured board.
circuit.style_p: Every symbol is a pour of gold-plated copper with a thin dark gap around its edge, the way a real layout keeps its parts apart. Tiny vias and solder pads dot the metal, and a few traces leave the shape and bend away at 45 degrees. Some parts are plated in a second metal such as pale silver or warm bronze, others are printed in white silkscreen ink or left as bare black board, which gives each shape a clear inside and outside even at small sizes.
circuit.make_p: A circuit board looks messy until you notice its rules, so the renderer follows them. Traces only turn at 45 degrees, parts keep their clearance, and faint copper lines run under the coloured coating behind each symbol in one of three routing patterns: free traces, parallel bus lines or a lattice of vias. Four mounting holes sit in the corners of every tile. The trick was restraint. A few traces make an icon look like hardware, and too many make it look like noise.
circuit.colours: ten board colours: blue, magenta, yellow, green, red, purple, teal, grey, orange and mint, with black kept for the darkest icons

critters.title: A Crowd of Tiny Monsters: Inventing the Critter Pals Icon Pack
critters.subtitle: Every icon on your phone, carried by a small creature with big eyes.
critters.description: How we invented the creatures of Critter Pals, an Android icon pack of 2,900+ cute elemental monster icons in ten element colours.
critters.intro: Somewhere between a sticker album and a creature collection lives Critter Pals. Instead of drawing a symbol and stopping there, we gave each one a small monster to wear it or hold it.
critters.style_h: A leaf frog hugging your camera
critters.style_p: A leaf frog hugs the camera, a spark bat flaps off with your mail, a cloud puff snoozes on your weather. Each creature is invented for this pack and looks like no existing game or franchise. Big eyes, rosy cheeks, a crest and a tail tip change with the element, so you can tell a flame creature from a frost one at a glance.
critters.make_h: Ten elements instead of ten colours
critters.make_p: Colour in this pack is a creature type. Tide, petal, sunny, sprout, ember, dusk, frosty, pebble, dune and puff each have their own palette, and an app gets the critter whose element sits nearest to the app's own colour. One dark coal critter looks after the black and charcoal apps. Every icon sits on a soft plate in the tint of its element, with a ring of dots, an element pattern or little sparkles, and a dark outline keeps every creature readable at launcher size.
critters.colours: ten element colours: tide, petal, sunny, sprout, ember, dusk, frosty, pebble, dune and puff, plus a dark coal critter

gems.title: Catching the Light: Cutting the Gemstones Icon Pack
gems.subtitle: A cut stone does one thing very well. We asked 2,900 icons to do the same.
gems.description: Why and how we made Gemstones, an Android icon pack of faceted gem icons in velvet, slate and enamel settings, with eleven stones and 2,900+ icons.
gems.intro: A cut stone catches the light and throws it back. That is the whole trick of a jewel, and it was our brief for Gemstones: an Android icon pack where every symbol looks like a small faceted stone in its own setting.
gems.style_h: Facets, bezels and a spark at the peak
gems.style_p: Every symbol is cut like a gem, with bright edges, darker faces and a tiny spark of light at its peak. Nothing is flat: each facet catches the light from a slightly different angle, and the stone glows softly against its setting. The settings are mixed across the set, dark velvet with a gold bezel, cool slate with a silver bezel, or glossy enamel with a fine gold ring.
gems.make_p: Our renderer takes a generic symbol and divides it into facets, then lights each facet from its own angle, like a lapidary turning a stone under a lamp. The settings behind the stones are deliberately deep and quiet, so the colour of the stone does the talking. The stones are an art style, not real gemstones, and they carry no value beyond your home screen. The hardest thing to get right was opal, which has to look milky without looking dirty.
gems.colours: ten stones and one black glass: sapphire, rose quartz, citrine, emerald, ruby, amethyst, aquamarine, onyx, topaz, opal and obsidian

japandi.title: Fewer Things, Better Things: The Thinking Behind Japandi
japandi.subtitle: A Japanese tea room and a Scandinavian living room agree on one thing, so we made an icon pack about it.
japandi.description: The story of Japandi, a calm minimal Android icon pack of stoneware and ink line icons on oak, linen and rice paper, with 2,900+ icons.
japandi.intro: Most icon packs try to make your screen louder. Japandi does the opposite. It borrows the calm of a Japanese tea room and a Scandinavian living room, where there are fewer things, better things and room around them.
japandi.style_h: Space is part of the design
japandi.style_p: Each symbol sits small on its plate, with a wide margin left empty on purpose. A crowded home screen stays uncluttered, and your wallpaper gets some air again. The plates are matte with soft corners, in three surfaces: oak with a fine grain, woven linen, or rice paper with long pale fibres. Symbols are glazed like hand-thrown stoneware and traced with one thin ink line.
japandi.make_p: Most of the work on Japandi was subtraction. Light falls gently from the top left, shadows are soft, and there is no gloss at all, because gloss is the first thing that makes a screen feel busy. We also tuned the palette down until nothing could shout. The ten tones are muted, and the persimmon is as loud as it gets. Whatever we have not drawn yet sits on a plain linen plate, so even the leftovers look intentional.
japandi.colours: ten muted tones: indigo, plum, sand, moss, clay, wisteria, tide, ash, persimmon and sage

kawaii.title: Little Faces for Every App: How Kawaii Friends Got Its Smile
kawaii.subtitle: Some icons just want to be friends. We gave 2,900 of them a face.
kawaii.description: How we drew Kawaii Friends, an Android icon pack of pastel blob icons with bead eyes, rosy cheeks and sparkles, in ten candy colours with 2,900+ icons.
kawaii.intro: Kawaii is the art of making something so cute that you cannot be annoyed at it. Kawaii Friends applies that to your launcher: plump pastel blobs with tiny faces, keeping you company on your home screen.
kawaii.style_h: Two bead eyes and a small smile
kawaii.style_p: Every symbol is a rounded blob outlined in a deeper tint of its own colour, with two bead eyes, a small smile and rosy cheeks. Sparkles and little hearts float around each one. The faces were invented for this pack and belong to no existing character. Each friend sits on a pastel plate with its own pattern, polka dots, fluffy clouds or twinkling stars, and the plate fades gently from one candy shade to a lighter one.
kawaii.make_p: The difference between a charming face and a creepy one is a few pixels. Eyes set a little too close together look worried, too far apart and they look vacant. We spent most of the time on proportions: the size of the cheeks, the distance between eyes and smile, how much outline a blob can take before it stops looking soft. Matching an app to a friend is done by job and by hue, so the messenger you know wears a friend that suits chatting, in a shade near its usual colour.
kawaii.colours: ten candy colours: peach, mint, lavender, sky, lemon, rose, aqua, lilac, apricot and cloud

origami.title: Fold Your Home Screen: Making the Origami Icon Pack
origami.subtitle: A sheet of coloured paper, folded once or twice, with the light catching every edge.
origami.description: The making of Origami, an Android icon pack of folded paper icons with crisp creases, flat facets and soft shadows, with ten paper colours and 2,900+ icons.
origami.intro: Origami starts with a flat square and ends with something that holds its shape. We wanted the same journey for icons, so Origami remakes your launcher as paper craft, with about 2,900 icons folded from coloured sheets.
origami.style_p: Each symbol is cut from coloured paper and creased into flat facets. One facet faces the light, the next turns away, and a fine crease marks the line between them. Paper fibre shows in the colour, and a pale edge runs round every sheet, so even the darkest paper keeps its outline. Parts of a symbol are separate sheets laid on top of each other, each throwing a soft shadow on the one below.
origami.make_h: Folds that a hand could make
origami.make_p: The rule we set ourselves was that every fold must be one a person could actually make. That is why the shapes are shallow and clean, like a card you could hold: a camera with a paper lens, an envelope with a folded flap, a pin standing up from its shadow. Behind every symbol lies a square sheet with its own folds: both diagonals, a cross fold or a single valley fold. The symbol for a busy app is picked by its job, and the paper by its usual colour.
origami.colours: ten paper colours from indigo and sakura to matcha, persimmon and saffron

spellbook.title: Your Phone as an Old Book of Spells: The Spellbook Icon Pack
spellbook.subtitle: Gold foil pressed into stained parchment, with a candle-warm glow behind it.
spellbook.description: How we made Spellbook, an Android icon pack of grimoire page icons with gold foil, stained parchment and stitched covers in ten colours, with 2,900+ icons.
spellbook.intro: Everyone who has opened a very old book knows the feeling: the weight of the cover, the smell of the pages, a hint that something in here is not quite ordinary. Spellbook tries to put that feeling behind every app icon.
spellbook.style_p: Each icon is a grimoire page. The symbol is pressed in gold foil with a dark ink edge, so it stays crisp at launcher size. The parchment is darkened toward the corners, ruled with a thin border and marked with a small ornament in every corner. Behind the gold, a candle-warm light seems to rise out of the paper. Round each page runs the binding: stitches in gold thread, a double gold rule and a wax seal pressed into the lower corner.
spellbook.make_p: Leather, woven cloth and dragon scale are the three cover materials, and every icon is bound in one of them. That variety matters, because a grid of identical books would look like a bookshelf in a catalogue. The wax seal colour is picked per cover so that it always stands out against it. The glow behind the foil was the final touch, and the one we changed most often. Too bright and the page looks lit by a phone, just right and it looks lit by a candle.
spellbook.colours: ten cover colours: navy, orchid, honey, forest, oxblood, plum, teal, ash, rust and jade

stained.title: Sunlight Through Lead: Making the Stained Glass Icon Pack
stained.subtitle: Sunlight in a cathedral window turns plain glass into colour. We tried to do that on a phone screen.
stained.description: The story of Stained Glass, an Android icon pack of tiny leaded windows with jewel tones, hammered glass and lead plates, with 2,900+ icons.
stained.intro: A stained glass window only looks alive when the sun is behind it. A phone screen is lit from behind all day, which made it an oddly perfect place for the idea. Stained Glass gives each of its 2,900+ icons the look of a tiny leaded window.
stained.style_p: Every symbol is cut from separate pieces of glass divided by thin lines of dark lead, the way a window maker would assemble it. The glass shows hammered ripples, a few trapped bubbles and a soft bloom where light spills over the lead, so each icon looks lit from behind. The symbol sits on a darker leaded plate and glows against it, and a frame of solid lead came runs around each plate.
stained.make_p: A window of one repeated pattern looks like wallpaper, so the plates alternate between three: a quarry lattice of small diamond panes, bullseye roundels, or plain lead with a heavy border. The lead lines had to be thin enough to keep small symbols readable and thick enough to read as lead, and that balance took many rounds. The bloom comes last: a faint glow that spreads from the glass over the lead, which is what sells the idea that the light comes from behind.
stained.colours: ten jewel tones: ruby, sapphire, emerald, amber, amethyst, teal, rose, citrine, smoke and ivory

stickers.title: The Sticker Sheet You Never Wanted to Finish: Die-cut Stickers
stickers.subtitle: Glossy vinyl, thick white borders and one corner that always peels.
stickers.description: How we made Die-cut Stickers, an Android icon pack of glossy vinyl sticker icons with white borders and holographic foil, in ten sheet colours with 2,900+ icons.
stickers.intro: Everyone had a sticker sheet that was too nice to use. Die-cut Stickers puts that feeling on your phone, with more than 2,900 icons that each look like a glossy vinyl sticker, trimmed around its own outline and pressed onto a bright sheet.
stickers.style_h: Bold ink, white border, peeling corner
stickers.style_p: Every symbol has a bold ink outline and a thick white die-cut border, just like a real sticker. One corner peels up a little, and a soft sheen runs across the vinyl from the top left. The shape stays easy to read, even small. The sticker is stuck on a bright matte sheet with a subtle pattern: tiny dots, a fine grid or diagonal stripes.
stickers.make_p: A page full of identical vinyl gets dull, so about one icon in six gets a holographic foil finish that shifts from pink to blue to gold. The effect is sparse on purpose. Just a few sparkles scattered through a full home screen feels like a treasure hunt, while too many turns it into a disco. The white border does a surprising amount of work: it separates each sticker from the sheet and from the wallpaper, so the grid stays readable.
stickers.colours: ten juicy sheet colours: blueberry, bubblegum, lemon, lime, cherry, grape, lagoon, slate, tangerine and mint

sushi.title: Served on a Plate: Plating 2,900 Icons in the Sushi Icon Pack
sushi.subtitle: Every app on your phone, served as a piece of sushi.
sushi.description: The story of Sushi, an Android icon pack that plates icons like nigiri with rice, topping and nori on lacquer, celadon and bamboo, with 2,900+ icons.
sushi.intro: A good sushi counter is a lesson in presentation: a neat bed of rice, a glossy topping, a thin strip of nori and a plate to set it on. Sushi dresses more than 2,900 icons the same way, and it is the most delicious-looking pack we have made.
sushi.style_p: Each symbol is made of white rice with visible grains, topped with salmon, tuna, tamago, avocado, cucumber, eel, shrimp, roe or pickled ginger, and bound with a band of dark nori. Look closely and you will see the marbling in the fish and the shine on the egg. Every piece sits on a plate with a small dab of wasabi and a curl of ginger on the side.
sushi.make_p: The plates come in three materials: black lacquer with a deep gloss, celadon ceramic with a fine crackle in the glaze, and woven bamboo with slats you can feel. The toppings double as the colour scheme, so the same symbol can be tuna-red, avocado-green or tamago-yellow. The glossy toppings were the challenge, because wet fish and boiled egg need different kinds of shine. We ended up with one sheen for fish, a harder one for egg, and a matte one for rice.
sushi.colours: ten toppings that make ten colour schemes: mackerel, shrimp, tamago, avocado, tuna, eel, roe, ginger, salmon and cucumber

voxel.title: Build Your Home Screen Out of Blocks: The Voxel World Icon Pack
voxel.subtitle: Small cubic sculptures, stacked from chunky pixels like a world you could mine and decorate.
voxel.description: How we made Voxel World, an Android icon pack of cubic block sculptures with pixel textures on sky, cave and dusk scenes, with 2,900+ icons.
voxel.intro: Block worlds taught a generation that a cube is enough to build anything. Voxel World turns more than 2,900 app icons into small cubic sculptures, stacked from chunky pixels like a world you could mine, climb and decorate.
voxel.style_p: Every symbol is assembled from cubes with their own tiny pixel texture: grass, stone, oak, sand, brick, ice, lava, water, crystal, snow and gold. Each cube has a lit top edge and a darker underside, so even a plain glyph looks like something you could pick up and place.
voxel.make_p: The plate behind each symbol is a small scene in three flavours: a bright sky with square clouds and a square sun, a dark cave of stone blocks with ore specks, or a dusk with stars and a moon. The three alternate across your apps, so the screen reads like a map and not a grid. The renderer works in real voxels, so symbols that have curves, such as a clock or a compass, are rebuilt to look good as stairs of cubes rather than blurred.
voxel.colours: ten block palettes: water, cherry, sand, grass, brick, amethyst, ice, stone, lava and snow

woodblock.title: A Drawing Cut Into a Plank: The Woodblock Print Icon Pack
woodblock.subtitle: Before there were screens there were woodblocks. We put the craft on your phone.
woodblock.description: The making of Woodblock Print, an Android icon pack of hand-printed ink icons on washi paper with a red seal and eleven traditional inks, with 2,900+ icons.
woodblock.intro: A woodblock print starts as a drawing cut into a plank, which is inked and pressed onto paper by hand. Woodblock Print carries that craft across more than 2,900 icons, and it is the quietest pack in our collection.
woodblock.style_h: Carved outline, flat ink, a seal in the corner
woodblock.style_p: Each symbol is drawn with a dark carved outline and filled with flat, muted ink. A faint wood grain shows through the colour, and one layer lands a hair off register, the way a real hand-pulled print never quite lines up. In one corner sits a small red seal square, left blank on purpose.
woodblock.make_p: The off-register layer is the detail we are proudest of. A perfect print looks like a computer made it, so we shift one ink layer by a hair and let the grain show through. The tiles come on three papers: cream washi, grey-green celadon and warm tan, each with soft fibres and slightly worn edges. Together they make a home screen that feels pulled from a portfolio rather than rendered by a machine.
woodblock.colours: eleven traditional inks: indigo, vermilion, ochre, moss, plum, slate, rust, teal, rose, celadon and sumi black
